disputed_claims.claim_from_lane: L05: cron scheduler subprocess's per-job acquire()/release_or_close() cycle causes frequent WAL-generation-ending closes 'many times/hour', invalidated if a handle is kept warm across a batch/tick
disputed_claims.dispute: Not disputed on the core mechanism, but L05's 'common case' framing needs one caveat: cron/scheduler.py runs jobs through a PERSISTENT parallel ThreadPoolExecutor (_parallel_pool, scheduler.py:508-977) that can run MULTIPLE jobs concurrently across threads, not strictly serial ticks. When 2+ jobs overlap in time, refcount does NOT hit 0 between them -- the registry's refcount is per-resolved-path across the whole process (hermes_state_registry.py:265-298), so overlapping jobs share one generation and only the LAST job's release() tears it down. This doesn't invalidate L05's frequency claim (overlaps are the exception, not norm, for typical cron cadences), but 'refcount hits 0 after each job' is only exactly true in the non-overlapping case, which L05 did already hedge as 'common case'.
disputed_claims.evidence: cron/scheduler.py:508-509 '_parallel_pool: Optional[ThreadPoolExecutor]' and :969-977 _get_parallel_pool() -- jobs can run in parallel worker threads, all funneling through the same acquire()/release_or_close() (scheduler.py:1687-1690, 1995-1997) against the process-global hermes_state_registry, so simultaneous job fires legitimately keep the generation's refcount above 0 across them.

confirmed_claims: L05 confirmed: cron/scheduler.py is registry-routed, not a bare SessionDB(). _open_cron_session_db() (scheduler.py:1673-1697) calls hermes_state_registry.acquire() (scheduler.py:1687,1690) and _finalize_cron_session() (scheduler.py:1913-1998) calls release_or_close() (scheduler.py:1995-1997). No scheduler-startup acquire() that stays open for the subprocess's whole life -- verified no persistent module-level SessionDB handle in scheduler.py outside these two call sites.

L05 confirmed: hermes_state_registry.release() (hermes_state_registry.py:265-298) decrements refcount and, when refcount<=0 (line 285), immediately admits a teardown OUTSIDE the lock (line 296-297) -- there is NO idle-keepalive/TTL/grace-period window found anywhere in hermes_state_registry.py (searched for grace|keepalive|idle|TTL|linger -- zero matches). In the common non-overlapping-job case, this does mean refcount reaches 0 and the generation physically closes after each job run, matching L05's claim.

L05 confirmed: SessionDB.close() semantics per hermes_state_registry.py:107-149 (_teardown/_admit_teardown_locked/_finish_teardown) tear down the connection physically on final release; this matches the docstring at hermes_state_registry.py:3-13 describing close-time WAL checkpoint behavior L05 cited from hermes_state.py.

L09 confirmed: acquire() DOES resolve the path (.resolve(), hermes_state_registry.py:194) and additionally checks (st_dev, st_ino) identity (lines 203-213) before keying/reusing a generation -- correctness of the registry's OWN dedup logic is sound, as L09 stated.

L09 confirmed, this is the real finding: cli.py:2838 constructs a bare, unregistered `self._session_db = SessionDB()` for the whole interactive CLI session (verified: 'from hermes_state import SessionDB' / 'self._session_db = SessionDB()' at cli.py:2837-2838). SessionDB.__init__ (hermes_state.py:420-421) stores `self.db_path = db_path or _default_db_path()` with NO .resolve() call at construction -- confirms L09's cited evidence verbatim.

L09 confirmed: delegate_tool.py's _open_child_session_db() (delegate_tool.py:83-104) reads the parent's UNRESOLVED `.db_path` attribute (line 102: `_parent_db_path = getattr(parent_session_db, 'db_path', None)`) and feeds it into `hermes_state_registry.acquire()` (line 103) to get a child handle. Because the parent's bare SessionDB() from cli.py:2838 was never registered with the registry (it has no entry in _generations), acquire() cannot find/reuse it -- it always opens a FRESH sqlite3 connection via _open_session_db() (hermes_state_registry.py:100-104,232-236) and creates/joins a NEW registry generation. This is a genuine second, independent writer connection object against the identical physical state.db file/inode as the parent's bare handle -- L09's core structural claim is correct and independently reproduced by reading the code.

L09 confirmed: delegate_tool.py's own code comment (lines 84-96) is self-aware of this being intentional-by-necessity (child must survive parent handle closing) but does NOT claim to dedupe against the parent's bare handle -- it explicitly documents wanting 'the same database FILE' not 'the same connection object', which is consistent with L09's read that this guarantees >=2 live writer handles whenever a bare-SessionDB CLI session delegates.
missing_gap: Neither L05 nor L09 quantifies which trigger (cron per-job close cycling vs. CLI-delegate double-writer) actually fires in a typical incident window versus being a theoretical hazard; also unaddressed by either lane: whether the cron subprocess's parallel pool (scheduler.py:508-977, found independently in this review) ever produces the INVERSE effect -- overlapping jobs keeping a generation's refcount pinned above 0 for longer stretches than L05's per-job model assumes, which would make cron's WAL-rotation frequency somewhat LOWER than 'many times/hour' during periods of concurrent job fires. This nuance does not overturn the theory but was not tested by any of L01-L19 as far as the consolidated summary shows.
verdict: Both L05's and L09's core mechanisms independently reverify true against source (repo actually resides at /home/ian-koratsky/Development/hermes-agent, not the path given in the task/consolidated doc, but the file:line citations are the same file structure and verified there). L05: cron/scheduler.py IS strictly registry-routed and DOES tear its generation down to a physical close whenever process-local refcount hits 0, which for non-overlapping job fires is after essentially every run -- confirmed, with a minor caveat that the scheduler's own persistent parallel ThreadPoolExecutor can let concurrent job fires share a generation and delay refcount-zero, meaning realized closure frequency during high-concurrency windows is somewhat lower than a strict 'per single job run' framing implies (does not invalidate the theory). L09: bare SessionDB() at cli.py:2838 truly bypasses the registry, and delegate_tool.py's _open_child_session_db() truly opens a second independent writer connection via acquire() against the same physical file/inode as the parent's unregistered handle -- confirmed exactly as claimed, this is the clearest, most concretely reproducible double-writer vector in the whole theory. I agree with the consolidated theory's overall shape.
